planting.note: Start indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost, or direct-sow once soil has warmed above 70°F; this Ghanaian heirloom needs a long, hot 90-100 day season to finish.

directions: This West African heirloom luffa is grown along the Gold Coast of Ghana for its dual harvest: young ridged fruit around 12 inches long can be sliced into soups and stews for a mild, slightly sweet flavor, while fruit left on the vine to fully mature and dry yields a fibrous sponge. Provide a sturdy trellis or arbor, since the vigorous vines can climb well over 15 feet in a single warm season. Give it full sun, evenly moist soil, and a long frost-free season of at least 90 days, switching to a phosphorus-heavy feed once flowering begins to support fruit set.

planting.note: Start indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost; this long-season type needs 110-130 warm days and benefits from the head start in all but the longest summers.

directions: This ridged luffa sets several fruits together at each node rather than singly, giving a concentrated flush of harvest when the small orb-shaped young gourds are ready to pick for stir-fries, curries, and soups. Left on the vine through its long 110-130 day season, the fruit dries into the familiar fibrous sponge once the skin turns brown and papery. Train the vigorous vines up a tall trellis in full sun to keep the ridged fruit straight and improve airflow, and keep soil consistently moist and mulched through the hot months it needs to finish.

planting.note: Start indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost in most regions; this extra-long selection needs a full 120-130 day warm season to mature fruit for sponges.

directions: Selected in Thailand for exceptional length, this smooth luffa can produce fruit exceeding four feet if left to mature, though it is best picked at 12-18 inches for cooking, when the flesh is still tender and mild like zucchini. Because it needs a long 120-130 day warm season and vines that can reach 15-25 feet, give it the tallest trellis or arbor available and start seed indoors where summers are short. Allow a portion of the crop to fully ripen and dry on the vine for use as natural bath and cleaning sponges, peeling and rinsing the skin away once it turns brown and papery.

planting.note: Direct-sow after soil has warmed above 70°F, or start indoors 4-6 weeks early for a head start; provide a sturdy trellis for the climbing vines.

directions: Big Top produces unusually large, softball-sized bitter melon with a rounded, heart-shaped profile and thick, bumpy dark green skin that ships and stores better than slender types. Grow it on a sturdy trellis in full sun and warm, fertile soil, harvesting fruit while it is still firm and bright green, since fruit left to yellow becomes markedly more bitter and eventually splits to release red-coated seeds. Regular picking every few days keeps the vine setting new fruit through the summer.

planting.note: Direct-sow after soil has warmed above 70°F, or start indoors 4-6 weeks early where summers are short; this is a long-season type needing 90-110 warm days.

directions: An Okinawan heirloom prized for unusually mild bitterness, Abashi produces cylindrical, deep green fruit 8-10 inches long that is popular sliced into stir-fries and Okinawan goya chanpuru. Give it a sturdy trellis and full sun, since this long-season type also performs well in a large container with a stake, provided the container gives roots room to run. Pick fruit while still firm and green for the mildest flavor and best texture; overripe fruit turns orange and splits.

planting.note: Direct-sow after soil has warmed above 70°F, or start indoors 4-6 weeks early; provide a tall trellis for this vigorous Thai type.

directions: This slender Thai type produces small, deeply ridged fruit with a notably assertive bitterness prized in Southeast Asian cooking. Provide a tall trellis in full sun and fertile, well-drained soil, and harvest young and often, since frequent picking of immature fruit keeps the vigorous vine flowering and setting new fruit. Left unpicked, fruit ripens to orange and splits open to reveal red-coated seeds, which can be saved after a short drying period.

planting.note: Direct-sow after soil has warmed above 70°F, or start indoors 4-6 weeks early; set plants slightly closer than most bitter melon and trellis from planting.

directions: Known in Okinawa as a 'longevity' vegetable, Ganjyu is an extra-large, light green type with deeply ridged skin and notably milder bitterness than typical dark green bitter melons. Set plants slightly closer than most bitter melon at 12-18 inches and provide a sturdy trellis at planting time, since the fast-growing vines need vertical support from early on. Keep soil consistently moist through flowering and fruiting, and encourage bee activity or hand-pollinate to ensure good fruit set on the long ridged fruit.

planting.note: Direct-sow after soil has warmed above 70°F, or start indoors 4-6 weeks early; train vines onto a tall trellis from planting time.

directions: Pearl Goya is an Okinawan selection that produces round, pearl-white fruit closer in shape to a golf ball than the typical elongated bitter melon, with a milder, almost umami flavor that suits simple soups. Grow it on a tall trellis in full sun with consistently moist, compost-rich soil, training vines vertically and pruning lateral shoots to keep air moving through the foliage. Harvest fruit while still pale and firm, picking early and often to extend the fruiting season.
